cards.explanation: The answer is the law. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus writing to Rome, says it plainly: "if you rely on the law and boast in God…" That's the thing this person leans on. I think leaning on something can feel like standing on solid ground, so Paul starts by naming it. Keep your eye on it, friends, because the law keeps coming back all through this passage.

The answer is True. Verse 19 says this person is convinced he's "…a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness…" Paul stacks up the titles one after another. I think that's on purpose, because the list is building toward something. Hold on, friends, the questions are coming.

The answer is "Do you not teach yourself." Paul asks, "…you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself?" After the whole list of titles, Paul turns it around and points it right back at the teacher. It lands like a mirror held up in the hallway. Everything before this was setup, and this is where it turns.

The answer is True. Verse 21 says it right out: "You who preach against stealing, do you steal?" Paul asks it as a question, so he's making the person look at himself. Nobody's getting a lecture, just a hard question. And it's the first of several in a row.

The answer is adultery. Verse 22 says, "You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery?" Then comes the idols question about robbing temples. Paul keeps firing these one after another, and I think the speed is part of the point. Same pattern every time: you say one thing, do you do the other?

The answer is "dishonor." Verse 23 says, "…do you dishonor God by breaking the law?" Paul ties the breaking of the law straight to how God is treated. This one lands heavy, so I'll say it once: it's a serious line. One word, big weight.

The answer is the Gentiles. Verse 24 says, "God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you." Paul introduces it with "As it is written…" so he's quoting Scripture. The Gentiles are the nations outside of Israel's covenant people. Paul puts the blasphemy among them and says it's because of you.

The answer is that you observe the law. Paul says, "Circumcision has value if you observe the law…" The value comes with a condition attached. Paul isn't throwing circumcision out, he's saying what it takes for it to mean something. Watch what he does with the flip side next, friends.

The answer is False. Paul says, "…if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision." So the sign doesn't still count when the law is broken. That's a big claim, and Paul says it flat out.

The answer is True. Verse 26 asks, "If a man who is not circumcised keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?" Paul asks it as a question, and the way he asks it points toward yes. It flips the whole picture upside down. I bet that surprised the people who first heard it.

The answer is "condemn." Verse 27 says the uncircumcised man who keeps the law "…will condemn you who, even though you have the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker." That's a strong word, and Paul picks it on purpose. The one who has all the outward stuff is the one being measured. Heavy line, friends, so it's worth slowing down on.

The answer is "Spirit." Verse 29 says, "…circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code." Paul points past the outside to the heart. Then he adds, "Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God." That's the answer to what counts.

The answer is False. Paul says, "Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God." The praise comes from God, not from people. That's a good place to land, and a good reminder that nobody has to impress the room.
